DAST pinpoints the exact vulnerable source line but never runs the application
SAST and DAST are identical in method and results
SAST needs a running application and cannot see source code

explanation.correct: SAST (white-box, no execution) finds issues early and names the code location but is prone to false positives; DAST (black-box, running app) finds runtime and configuration flaws but cannot point to the exact source line.

distractors.B: This reverses them — DAST runs the app and does NOT identify source lines.
distractors.C: They are fundamentally different techniques (static white-box vs dynamic black-box).
distractors.D: This reverses the definitions — SAST analyzes source WITHOUT running the app.

explanation.exam_pattern: SAST = early, code-level, more false positives; DAST = runtime/black-box, finds config flaws but no code location.

references: CompTIA CySA+ CS0-003 Objective 2.2 — SAST vs DAST (trade-offs)

questions.stem: Two vulnerabilities are identical except that one needs no special conditions to exploit, while the other works only if the attacker first wins a timing race condition. How does CVSS v3.1 reflect the easier one, and what is the score effect?

options.text: Privileges Required: High, which raises the base score
Attack Complexity: High, which raises the base score
Attack Complexity: Low, which lowers the base score
Attack Complexity: Low, which raises the base score

explanation.correct: No special conditions = Attack Complexity: Low, meaning reliably repeatable exploitation, which increases the CVSS base score. The race-condition case would be AC:High and score lower.

distractors.A: This scenario is about complexity, not privileges, and PR:High actually lowers the score.
distractors.B: The easy case is AC:Low, not High; AC:High (special conditions) LOWERS the score.
distractors.C: AC:Low raises, not lowers, the base score.

explanation.exam_pattern: CVSS AC:Low (no special conditions) = easier = higher score; AC:High (e.g., race condition) lowers it.

references: CompTIA CySA+ CS0-003 Objective 2.3 — CVSS base metrics (Attack Complexity)
FIRST CVSS v3.1 Specification

questions.stem: A vulnerability can be exploited only if a victim opens a malicious document. Which CVSS v3.1 base metric value captures this, and how does it affect the score versus a flaw needing no victim action?

options.text: User Interaction: None, raising the score
Attack Vector: Physical, raising the score
User Interaction: Required, lowering the score relative to UI:None

explanation.correct: Needing a victim to act sets User Interaction: Required, which lowers the base score compared with UI:None (no victim action needed), because exploitation depends on someone else's behavior.

distractors.A: The flaw needs victim action, so UI is Required, not None.
distractors.B: Scope: Changed describes cross-boundary impact, not victim interaction, and does not lower the score for this reason.
distractors.C: Requiring a user to open a file is not Attack Vector: Physical, and that would not apply here.

explanation.exam_pattern: Needs victim action = UI:Required (lower score); no action needed = UI:None (higher score).

references: CompTIA CySA+ CS0-003 Objective 2.3 — CVSS base metrics (User Interaction)
FIRST CVSS v3.1 Specification

questions.stem: Beyond the base score, a team wants their CVSS rating to rise when a working, weaponized exploit becomes publicly available and fall when a vendor patch ships. Which CVSS metric group captures these conditions that change over time?

options.text: The Temporal metric group (e.g., Exploit Code Maturity, Remediation Level)

explanation.correct: Temporal metrics (Exploit Code Maturity, Remediation Level, Report Confidence) adjust the score for conditions that change over time — a public weaponized exploit raises it; an official fix lowers it.

distractors.B: Attack Vector is a single base metric, not the time-varying group.
distractors.C: CIA impacts are part of the base score and do not track exploit/patch status.
distractors.D: Base metrics are intrinsic and constant; they do not vary with exploit availability.

explanation.exam_pattern: Exploit availability / patch status over time = CVSS Temporal metrics.

references: CompTIA CySA+ CS0-003 Objective 2.3 — CVSS metric groups (Temporal)
FIRST CVSS v3.1 Specification

questions.stem: Two hosts share the same CVSS base score of 7.5. One is a sandbox holding no data; the other stores regulated customer financial records. Which factor should raise the second host's remediation priority?

options.text: The alphabetical order of the hostnames
Nothing — identical base scores must be treated identically
Asset criticality and data sensitivity (environmental/business context)

explanation.correct: Prioritization weighs business context: the host with regulated financial data is a far more valuable target with greater impact if exploited, so asset criticality/data sensitivity (CVSS environmental context) elevates its priority.

distractors.A: Hostname order is arbitrary and irrelevant to risk.
distractors.B: Equal base scores do not mean equal risk; context differentiates them.
distractors.C: The plugin ID is scan metadata, not a risk factor.

explanation.exam_pattern: Tailor priority with asset criticality/data sensitivity (CVSS Environmental), not base score alone.

references: CompTIA CySA+ CS0-003 Objective 2.3 — Prioritization (asset criticality, CVSS Environmental)

questions.stem: After mitigating what it can, a company buys a cyber-insurance policy to cover the residual financial loss from a potential breach. Which risk-response strategy is this?

explanation.correct: Shifting the financial consequences of a risk to a third party (an insurer) is risk transference; it addresses the residual risk left after other controls are applied.

distractors.A: Avoidance eliminates the risky activity/exposure entirely, not just shifts its cost.
distractors.B: The technical mitigation is already done; insurance covers what remains, so this is not patching.
distractors.C: Acceptance retains the loss and takes no action; insurance instead shifts the loss.

explanation.exam_pattern: Shifting residual financial risk to a third party (insurance) = risk transference.

references: CompTIA CySA+ CS0-003 Objective 2.5 — Risk response (transfer/avoid/accept/mitigate)

questions.stem: To reduce the chance that a bad patch disrupts the whole fleet, an admin deploys a critical update first to a small pilot group, monitors for problems, then expands to the rest. Which practice is this?

options.text: Rolling the patch back before testing it

explanation.correct: A phased or ring/canary rollout validates the patch on a small group first, limiting the blast radius if it causes problems before it reaches the full environment.

distractors.A: Simultaneous deployment maximizes the blast radius if the patch is faulty.
distractors.B: Rolling back before any testing defeats the purpose of validating the patch.
distractors.C: Skipping the patch leaves the vulnerability unaddressed.

explanation.exam_pattern: Pilot group first, monitor, then expand = phased/ring (canary) deployment.

references: CompTIA CySA+ CS0-003 Objective 2.5 — Patch management (phased deployment)

questions.stem: Before applying a kernel update to a critical production server, the change ticket documents the exact steps to restore the previous state if the update fails. What is this element called?

explanation.correct: A rollback/backout plan documents how to revert a change if it fails, limiting downtime and risk; it is a standard element of change management for critical systems.

distractors.A: Chain of custody tracks evidence handling, not change reversal.
distractors.B: A retention schedule governs how long data is kept.
distractors.D: A disclosure policy governs reporting vulnerabilities, not reverting a change.

explanation.exam_pattern: Documented way to revert a failed change = rollback/backout plan (change management).

references: CompTIA CySA+ CS0-003 Objective 2.5 — Change management (rollback/backout planning)

questions.stem: Which TWO controls specifically help prevent cross-site request forgery (CSRF)? (Choose two.)

options.text: Forcing a longer password minimum length

explanation.correct: Unpredictable per-session anti-CSRF tokens (that attackers cannot guess) and SameSite cookies (which stop the browser from sending session cookies on cross-site requests) both defeat CSRF.

distractors.A: Password length does not stop a forged request against an already-authenticated session.
distractors.D: Parameterized queries prevent SQL injection, not forged cross-site requests.

explanation.exam_pattern: CSRF defenses = anti-CSRF (synchronizer) tokens + SameSite cookies (not SQLi/password controls).

references: CompTIA CySA+ CS0-003 Objective 2.4 — Secure coding (CSRF mitigation)
OWASP CSRF Prevention Cheat Sheet

questions.stem: A web app fetches a user-supplied URL on the server side. An attacker supplies http://169.254.169.254/ and retrieves cloud instance credentials. Which vulnerability class is this, and a key mitigation?

options.text: Server-side request forgery (SSRF); validate/allowlist outbound destinations and block the metadata endpoint
Broken authentication; fix by enforcing MFA
SQL injection; fix with prepared statements
Cross-site scripting; fix with output encoding

explanation.correct: Coercing the server to request an attacker-chosen URL — here the cloud metadata address 169.254.169.254 — is SSRF; mitigations include allowlisting outbound destinations and blocking access to the metadata endpoint.

distractors.B: MFA protects login, not a server making an attacker-controlled outbound request.
distractors.C: SQL injection targets a database query, not server-side URL fetching.
distractors.D: XSS executes script in a victim's browser; output encoding does not stop a server-side fetch.

explanation.exam_pattern: Server fetches an attacker-controlled URL (e.g., cloud metadata 169.254.169.254) = SSRF; allowlist/block metadata.

references: CompTIA CySA+ CS0-003 Objective 2.4 — Secure coding (SSRF)
OWASP Top 10 A10:2021 — Server-Side Request Forgery

questions.stem: A code review finds a database password and an API key written directly into source code and committed to the repository. What is the best remediation?

options.text: Remove the secrets from code, load them at runtime from a secrets manager/vault, and rotate the exposed credentials
Base64-encode the secrets in the source
Rename the variables that hold the secrets
Add a code comment warning not to share the file

explanation.correct: Hardcoded secrets must be removed from code and version history, supplied at runtime from a secrets manager/vault, and rotated, because anything committed to the repo should be treated as compromised.

distractors.B: Base64 is reversible encoding, not protection; the secret is still exposed.
distractors.C: Renaming variables leaves the secrets in the code and its history.
distractors.D: A comment does nothing to protect already-exposed secrets.

explanation.exam_pattern: Hardcoded secrets = remove from code, use a secrets manager/vault, and rotate the exposed credentials.

references: CompTIA CySA+ CS0-003 Objective 2.4 — Secure coding (secrets management)
OWASP Top 10 A02:2021 — Cryptographic Failures (hardcoded credentials)

questions.stem: A SOC uses the SANS six-step handling process (Preparation, Identification, Containment, Eradication, Recovery, Lessons Learned). Which step corresponds to NIST's 'Detection and Analysis' — confirming an event is a real incident and determining its scope?

explanation.correct: In the SANS model, Identification is where responders validate that an event is a genuine incident and scope it — the same work NIST SP 800-61 places in Detection and Analysis.

distractors.A: Containment limits spread AFTER the incident is identified.
distractors.C: Eradication removes the threat after containment.
distractors.D: Recovery restores normal operations near the end of the process.

explanation.exam_pattern: SANS 'Identification' = NIST 'Detection and Analysis' (confirm and scope the incident).

references: CompTIA CySA+ CS0-003 Objective 3.2 — Incident response process (SANS PICERL vs NIST)
NIST SP 800-61 — Computer Security Incident Handling Guide

questions.stem: An adversary emails a weaponized PDF to employees. In the Lockheed Martin Cyber Kill Chain, transmitting the weaponized payload to the target is which phase?

explanation.correct: Delivery is the transmission of the weaponized payload to the victim — for example a phishing email, malicious link, or infected USB.

distractors.A: Installation is implanting a backdoor after successful exploitation.
distractors.B: Weaponization is building/coupling the payload before it is sent, not transmitting it.
distractors.D: Actions on Objectives is the final goal, such as exfiltration.

explanation.exam_pattern: Transmitting the weapon to the victim (phishing email, malicious USB) = Delivery.

references: CompTIA CySA+ CS0-003 Objective 3.1 — Attack frameworks (Cyber Kill Chain: Delivery)
Lockheed Martin — Cyber Kill Chain

questions.stem: A ransomware outage threatens to halt order processing. Which plan specifically addresses keeping critical business functions operating during the disruption?

explanation.correct: The business continuity plan keeps critical business functions running (often via alternate processes) during a disruption, whereas the DRP focuses on restoring IT systems afterward.

distractors.B: An AUP defines acceptable use of resources and is unrelated to continuity.
distractors.C: The DRP focuses on recovering/restoring IT systems and infrastructure after a disaster.
distractors.D: The IRP governs detecting and handling the security incident, not sustaining operations.

explanation.exam_pattern: Keep critical business functions running during disruption = BCP; restore IT after disaster = DRP; handle the incident = IRP.

references: CompTIA CySA+ CS0-003 Objective 3.3 — Incident management (BCP vs DRP vs IRP)

questions.stem: Using the Diamond Model, an analyst starts from a known malicious C2 IP (infrastructure) and queries passive DNS and registration data to uncover the adversary and additional capabilities. This analytic move across the model's vertices is called...

explanation.correct: Pivoting is the Diamond Model technique of using one known feature (e.g., infrastructure) to discover others (adversary, capability, victim), expanding understanding of the intrusion.

distractors.B: Containment is an incident-response action, not Diamond-Model analysis.
distractors.C: Weaponization is an attacker Cyber Kill Chain step, not a Diamond Model analytic technique.
distractors.D: Order of volatility governs the sequence of evidence collection, not intrusion analysis.

explanation.exam_pattern: Using one known Diamond vertex (e.g., infrastructure) to discover another (adversary/capability) = pivoting.

references: CompTIA CySA+ CS0-003 Objective 3.1 — Attack frameworks (Diamond Model: pivoting)

questions.stem: Before analyzing a suspect hard drive, an examiner connects it through a device that permits reading but prevents any writes to the original media. What is this device?

explanation.correct: A write blocker allows read-only access to source media during imaging, preventing any modification so the evidence stays forensically sound and admissible.

distractors.A: A USB hub only adds ports and offers no write protection.
distractors.B: A KVM switch shares a keyboard, video, and mouse across computers; it provides no write protection.
distractors.D: A network tap copies network traffic; it does not protect a disk.

explanation.exam_pattern: Read-only acquisition that prevents altering the source disk = write blocker.

references: CompTIA CySA+ CS0-003 Objective 3.2 — Forensics/evidence acquisition (write blocker)

questions.stem: Per NIST SP 800-61 terminology, a server log shows reconnaissance scanning that suggests an attack on a web app may be coming. Is this a precursor or an indicator, and why?

options.text: An indicator, because the attack has already succeeded
A precursor, because the breach is confirmed and ongoing
A precursor, because it is a sign that an incident may occur in the future
An indicator, because the system has already been eradicated

explanation.correct: A precursor is a sign that an incident may occur in the future; reconnaissance scanning hints at a possible upcoming attack but is not itself evidence that one has happened.

distractors.A: Nothing shows the attack succeeded; a sign of a POSSIBLE future attack is a precursor, not an indicator.
distractors.B: A precursor concerns a possible future event, not a confirmed ongoing breach.
distractors.D: Eradication has not occurred, and this is not evidence of a current incident.

explanation.exam_pattern: Precursor = sign an incident MAY occur later; indicator = sign an incident may be occurring or has occurred.

references: CompTIA CySA+ CS0-003 Objective 3.2 — Detection and analysis (precursors vs indicators)
NIST SP 800-61 — precursors and indicators

questions.stem: To prove that a now-deleted malicious executable actually ran on a Windows host, which forensic artifact is most useful?

explanation.correct: Prefetch files record program execution (name, run count, timestamps) and persist even after the executable is deleted, providing strong evidence that a binary ran.

distractors.A: The print spooler tracks print jobs, not arbitrary program runs.
distractors.B: Wallpaper settings do not record program execution.
distractors.C: The display driver version says nothing about what executed.

explanation.exam_pattern: Evidence a program executed (even if deleted) = Prefetch (and related artifacts like Shimcache/Amcache).

references: CompTIA CySA+ CS0-003 Objective 3.2 — Forensic analysis (Windows execution artifacts)

questions.stem: An analyst has a RAM image from a compromised host and needs to list the processes that were running, their network connections, and any injected code at capture time. Which approach fits?

options.text: A memory-forensics framework such as Volatility

explanation.correct: Memory-forensics tools like Volatility parse a RAM capture to reconstruct running processes, network connections, loaded modules, and injected code that never touch disk.

distractors.A: A defragmenter reorganizes disk storage and cannot parse a memory image.
distractors.B: A password manager stores credentials; it does not analyze RAM.
distractors.D: A CRC is an integrity check, not a memory analysis.

explanation.exam_pattern: Analyze a RAM capture (processes, connections, injected code) = memory forensics (e.g., Volatility).

references: CompTIA CySA+ CS0-003 Objective 3.2 — Forensic analysis (memory/RAM analysis)

questions.stem: Responders must contain a compromised server that likely holds important volatile evidence. Which containment action best stops attacker access while preserving that evidence?

options.text: Immediately wipe and reimage the disk
Leave it fully connected and keep watching
Network-isolate the host (e.g., move it to a quarantine VLAN) while leaving it powered on

explanation.correct: Isolating the host (quarantine VLAN, port block) cuts off the attacker while keeping the system powered on so volatile evidence in RAM is preserved for acquisition.

distractors.A: Wiping/reimaging destroys all evidence and is an eradication step, not evidence-preserving containment.
distractors.B: Pulling power destroys volatile memory evidence (running processes, keys, network state).
distractors.C: Leaving it connected allows continued attacker access and ongoing damage.

explanation.exam_pattern: Preserve volatile evidence AND stop access = isolate (quarantine) while powered on; don't power off or wipe first.

references: CompTIA CySA+ CS0-003 Objective 3.2 — Containment strategy (evidence preservation vs damage)

questions.stem: Investigation confirms an attacker stole domain and service-account credentials. Which TWO actions most directly remove the attacker's stolen access? (Choose two.)

options.text: Change the company logo on the intranet
Invalidate active sessions and tokens (and reset the Kerberos krbtgt where domain-wide compromise is suspected)
Reset/rotate the affected account passwords and disable compromised accounts

explanation.correct: Resetting/rotating and disabling the compromised credentials removes the attacker's keys, and invalidating live sessions/tokens (and krbtgt for domain-wide compromise) revokes access already granted with them.

distractors.A: Changing a logo has no security effect on stolen credentials.
distractors.C: Defragmenting the disk does not revoke any stolen access.

explanation.exam_pattern: Stolen credentials = reset/rotate + disable accounts AND invalidate sessions/tokens (revoke access).

references: CompTIA CySA+ CS0-003 Objective 3.2 — Eradication (credential reset/rotation, session invalidation)

questions.stem: To cut off malware's command-and-control without immediately taking infected endpoints offline, the team redirects the known malicious C2 domains to a controlled internal address. What is this containment technique?

explanation.correct: DNS sinkholing redirects malicious domains to a controlled address, severing the C2 channel and letting responders identify infected hosts (which now beacon to the sinkhole) without taking endpoints down.

distractors.A: A full-interruption test halts systems to validate DR, not to block C2.
distractors.C: A tabletop is a discussion-based rehearsal, not an active containment control.
distractors.D: A write blocker is a forensic acquisition device, not a network control.

explanation.exam_pattern: Redirect/block malicious C2 domains at DNS/egress to sever C2 = DNS sinkholing (containment).

references: CompTIA CySA+ CS0-003 Objective 3.2 — Containment (DNS sinkhole / egress blocking of C2)

questions.stem: During recovery, the team must restore a server from backup. The initial compromise is estimated to have occurred three weeks ago. Which backup should they restore from?

options.text: The most recent nightly backup, taken last night
Any backup, since all backups are identical
A verified-clean backup taken before the estimated compromise date, after confirming it is free of attacker artifacts
No backup — restoration is unnecessary after a breach

explanation.correct: Restoration must use a known-good backup from before the compromise and verified clean; a backup taken after the intrusion likely contains the attacker's implants and would reinfect the system.

distractors.A: Last night's backup is post-compromise and probably contains the attacker's persistence.
distractors.B: Backups differ over time; a post-compromise backup is tainted.
distractors.D: Restoring a clean state is a core recovery step after eradication.

explanation.exam_pattern: Restore from a verified-clean backup predating the compromise; a post-compromise backup can reintroduce the threat.

references: CompTIA CySA+ CS0-003 Objective 3.2 — Recovery (restore from known-good/clean backups)

questions.stem: A critical patch requires taking a 24/7 manufacturing line offline for three hours, which would stop production entirely. Which inhibitor to remediation does this represent?

explanation.correct: The obstacle is the downtime needed to apply the fix, which halts operations — a business process interruption. The patch itself works; the problem is the required outage.

distractors.A: Nothing indicates the system is vendor-closed; the blocker is the production outage.
distractors.B: Degrading functionality is when the fix itself breaks a needed feature; here the patch works but needs downtime.
distractors.D: An MOU is an inter-party agreement, not a downtime constraint.

explanation.exam_pattern: Required downtime that halts operations = business process interruption (vs degrading functionality = the fix breaks a feature).

references: CompTIA CySA+ CS0-003 Objective 4.1 — Inhibitors to remediation (business process interruption)

questions.stem: A vulnerability sits on a 15-year-old application server running an unsupported OS the vendor no longer updates, and no compatible patch exists. Which inhibitor to remediation best describes the obstacle?

explanation.correct: An aged, unsupported platform with no available patch is a legacy-system inhibitor; such systems typically require compensating controls (isolation, monitoring) because they cannot be patched.

distractors.B: No patch exists to break a feature; the system is simply too old/unsupported to patch.
distractors.C: The blocker is the obsolete platform, not downtime needed to apply a fix.
distractors.D: No contractual service level is described; the obstacle is the unsupported platform itself.

explanation.exam_pattern: Old, unsupported, unpatchable platform = legacy-system inhibitor (handle with compensating controls).

references: CompTIA CySA+ CS0-003 Objective 4.1 — Inhibitors to remediation (legacy systems)

questions.stem: Leadership decides to defer remediating a medium-severity finding for six months. To report this responsibly, what should the vulnerability report include?

options.text: Silently mark it 'fixed' to close it out
A documented, approved risk exception naming the risk owner, justification, compensating controls, and an expiration/review date
Raise the finding's CVSS score so it appears handled
Simply delete the finding from the report

explanation.correct: Deferred remediation is recorded as a formal, approved risk exception with an accountable owner, justification, interim compensating controls, and a review/expiration date — preserving the audit trail and governance.

distractors.A: Marking an open issue 'fixed' is false reporting.
distractors.C: Inflating the CVSS score does not record or govern the deferral decision.
distractors.D: Deleting the finding hides real risk and breaks the audit trail.

explanation.exam_pattern: Deferred remediation = documented, time-bound risk exception (owner, justification, compensating controls, expiration).

references: CompTIA CySA+ CS0-003 Objective 4.1 — Vulnerability reporting (risk exceptions/acceptance documentation)

questions.stem: A U.S. publicly traded company determines that a cybersecurity incident is material. Under the SEC cybersecurity disclosure rules, within what timeframe must it generally file a Form 8-K (Item 1.05)?

options.text: Four business days after determining the incident is material
Only at the next annual 10-K filing
Within one hour of any security alert

explanation.correct: The SEC rule requires an Item 1.05 Form 8-K generally within four business days after the registrant determines the incident is material (the clock starts at the materiality determination, not at discovery).

distractors.B: Material incidents require a prompt 8-K, not waiting for the annual 10-K.
distractors.C: 180 days far exceeds the four-business-day requirement.
distractors.D: No SEC rule imposes a one-hour deadline, and the clock starts at the materiality determination, not any alert.

explanation.exam_pattern: SEC material cyber incident → Form 8-K Item 1.05 within four business days of the materiality determination.

references: CompTIA CySA+ CS0-003 Objective 4.2 — Legal/regulatory reporting (SEC Form 8-K Item 1.05)
SEC Release 33-11216 (Cybersecurity Disclosure)

questions.stem: A U.S. healthcare provider confirms a breach of unsecured protected health information (PHI) affecting 4,000 patients. Under the HIPAA Breach Notification Rule, affected individuals must be notified without unreasonable delay and no later than...

options.text: Only after law enforcement closes its case

explanation.correct: HIPAA requires notifying affected individuals without unreasonable delay and no later than 60 calendar days from discovery of the breach; breaches affecting 500+ also require notifying HHS and the media.

distractors.A: Notification cannot wait indefinitely on law enforcement; a limited delay may be requested, but the rule still applies.
distractors.B: HIPAA does not set a 24-hour individual-notification deadline; 60 days is the outer limit.
distractors.C: Two years far exceeds the 60-day requirement.

explanation.exam_pattern: HIPAA breach → notify individuals without unreasonable delay, at most 60 calendar days from discovery (500+ also notify HHS/media).

references: CompTIA CySA+ CS0-003 Objective 4.2 — Legal/regulatory reporting (HIPAA Breach Notification Rule)
HHS — Breach Notification Rule (45 CFR 164.404)

questions.stem: After a ransomware incident, an organization holds a cyber-insurance policy. Which TWO are valid reasons to notify the insurance carrier promptly? (Choose two.)

options.text: Timely notice is often a condition of coverage under the policy
The insurer will issue the company's public press release
The insurer may require the use of approved incident-response/forensic vendors
Notifying the insurer removes the need for legal counsel

explanation.correct: Cyber policies commonly make prompt notification a condition of coverage, and insurers often direct claimants to pre-approved IR/forensic/legal panel vendors — so the carrier is an important early stakeholder.

distractors.B: Public statements are handled by the organization's PR and legal teams, not the insurer.
distractors.D: Legal counsel is still required; the insurer does not replace it.

explanation.exam_pattern: Notify the cyber-insurer promptly — coverage can depend on timely notice and insurers may mandate approved IR vendors.

references: CompTIA CySA+ CS0-003 Objective 4.2 — Incident reporting (stakeholder identification; third parties/insurer)

questions.stem: A SOC wants a metric for the average time from detecting an incident to successfully containing it (stopping its spread). Which KPI is this?

explanation.correct: Mean time to contain measures how quickly the team halts an incident's spread after detection; it sits between detection and full remediation on the response timeline.

distractors.A: MTBF is a hardware reliability metric, not an incident-response timing metric.
distractors.B: MTTD measures time until detection, which ends where MTTC begins.
distractors.D: Scan coverage measures how much of the estate is scanned, not containment speed.

explanation.exam_pattern: Detection → containment (spread stopped) = mean time to contain (MTTC).

references: CompTIA CySA+ CS0-003 Objective 4.2 — Metrics and KPIs (MTTC vs MTTD/MTTR)

questions.stem: A SOC manager finds analysts are overwhelmed and wants a metric showing how many alerts turn out to be benign, so detections can be tuned. Which metric fits?

explanation.correct: The false-positive rate — the share of alerts that are benign — directly measures detection quality and alert fatigue, guiding which rules to tune or suppress.

distractors.A: MTTD measures detection speed, not alert quality.
distractors.B: Scan coverage measures how much of the estate is scanned, not alert accuracy.
distractors.C: An asset count is inventory size, unrelated to alert accuracy.

explanation.exam_pattern: Share of alerts that are benign = false-positive rate (drives detection tuning, reduces alert fatigue).

references: CompTIA CySA+ CS0-003 Objective 4.2 — Metrics and KPIs (false-positive rate / detection quality)

questions.stem: Scans repeatedly reveal publicly exposed cloud storage buckets created through infrastructure-as-code (IaC) templates. Which team should the analyst collaborate with to fix the root cause?

options.text: The cloud/DevOps engineering team that owns the IaC templates and pipeline

explanation.correct: Because the exposure is generated by the IaC templates, fixing the templates and pipeline guardrails with the cloud/DevOps team corrects the root cause and stops new buckets from being misconfigured.

distractors.B: Facilities manages buildings, not cloud configurations.
distractors.C: Media relations handles external messaging, not cloud remediation.
distractors.D: Accounts payable handles finances, not infrastructure-as-code.

explanation.exam_pattern: Recurring cloud misconfiguration from IaC → collaborate with the cloud/DevOps team to fix the templates/pipeline (root cause).

references: CompTIA CySA+ CS0-003 Objective 4.1 — Collaboration with internal teams (cloud/DevOps)

questions.stem: An external auditor requests proof that the organization is meeting a regulatory requirement to remediate critical vulnerabilities on time. What should the security team provide?

options.text: Reports mapping remediation evidence (scan results, timelines, documented exceptions) to the relevant compliance controls/requirements
A copy of the attacker's malware sample
The analysts' personal opinions with no supporting data

explanation.correct: Auditors and regulators need evidence tied to the specific control/requirement: scan results, remediation timelines against SLAs, and any documented exceptions, mapped to the applicable framework.

distractors.B: Sharing a malware sample is inappropriate and does not prove compliance.
distractors.C: Raw packet captures do not demonstrate remediation compliance.
distractors.D: Unsupported opinions are not audit evidence.

explanation.exam_pattern: Audience = auditors/regulators → provide evidence mapped to the applicable controls/requirements (scan data, timelines, exceptions).

references: CompTIA CySA+ CS0-003 Objective 4.1/4.2 — Stakeholder communication (auditors/regulators; compliance evidence)

questions.stem: Investigating a suspected macro attack, an analyst wants the full command line of every process launched on a Windows host. Which Security event ID should they review?

options.text: 4663 (an attempt was made to access an object)

explanation.correct: Event ID 4688 logs process creation; with 'Include command line in process-creation events' enabled it captures the full command line, exposing encoded or living-off-the-land invocations.

distractors.A: 4624 records a successful logon session, not process execution or its command line.
distractors.B: 4720 records creation of a user account, unrelated to spawned-process command lines.
distractors.D: 4663 records an attempt to access an object such as a file, not process creation.

explanation.exam_pattern: Need the command line of spawned Windows processes = Event ID 4688 (with command-line auditing).

references: CS0-003 1.1 - Logging/endpoint telemetry (Windows Event IDs)

questions.stem: Reviewing an external scan, an analyst finds a company server accepting inbound connections from the internet on TCP 3389. Which exposed service creates this risk?

explanation.correct: TCP 3389 is RDP; exposing it to the internet invites credential brute-forcing and is a common ransomware initial-access vector.

distractors.A: DNS uses UDP/TCP 53, not 3389.
distractors.C: SSH listens on TCP 22, not 3389.
distractors.D: SMB uses TCP 445 (and legacy 139), not 3389.

explanation.exam_pattern: 3389 = RDP; internet-exposed RDP is a top initial-access risk.

references: CS0-003 1.1 - Common ports and protocols

questions.stem: A workstation that normally uploads under 10 MB daily sends 4 GB over HTTPS to an unfamiliar host at 3 a.m. Which analytic approach best flags this as suspicious?

options.text: Verify the destination's TLS certificate is valid
Compare current flow volume against the host's established baseline
Check that endpoint antivirus signatures are current

explanation.correct: Anomaly detection compares observed behavior to a learned baseline; a large off-hours transfer that deviates sharply from normal volume is a strong exfiltration indicator regardless of the protocol used.

distractors.A: A valid certificate does not make a 400x volume spike to an unknown host benign; attackers use valid TLS.
distractors.C: Port 443 being 'expected' is exactly why exfiltration hides there; the port alone proves nothing.
distractors.D: Current AV signatures do nothing to explain anomalous data-egress volume.

explanation.exam_pattern: Deviation from an established baseline (volume/time) = anomaly worth investigating, even over normal ports.

references: CS0-003 1.1 - Baselines and anomaly detection

questions.stem: After an IOC is published, an analyst must find which internal hosts contacted a malicious IP over the past 30 days, but full packet storage is unavailable. Which source fits?

explanation.correct: Flow records store compact connection metadata (source, destination, ports, bytes, timestamps) at low storage cost, making them ideal for long-retention retrospective lookups of who contacted a given IP.

distractors.A: Full packet capture is storage-heavy and rarely retained for 30 days; it is also unnecessary when only connection metadata is needed.
distractors.B: Email gateway logs cover mail flow, not arbitrary IP-to-IP connections.
distractors.C: EDR memory dumps show host process state, not a month of network conversations.

explanation.exam_pattern: Historical 'who talked to this IP' with limited storage = NetFlow/flow data, not full pcap.

references: CS0-003 1.1 - Network telemetry (flow vs. full capture)

questions.stem: An EDR alert shows winword.exe spawning cmd.exe, which then launched powershell.exe. Which observation most strongly suggests a malicious document executed?

options.text: The size of the Word document

explanation.correct: A productivity app such as Word spawning a shell and then PowerShell is an abnormal process lineage characteristic of malicious macros; normal editing never creates that chain.

distractors.A: PowerShell's standard path is not itself suspicious; the spawning relationship is the indicator.
distractors.B: Document size does not indicate whether a macro executed.
distractors.C: Group membership affects privileges, not whether the process chain is anomalous.

explanation.exam_pattern: Office app -> shell -> PowerShell lineage = malicious-macro behavior.

references: CS0-003 1.2 - Host indicators (process lineage)

questions.stem: While building an incident timeline, an analyst finds firewall, IDS, and server events appear out of order even though all were captured. What must be corrected to fix correlation?

explanation.correct: Reliable cross-source correlation depends on synchronized clocks; without consistent NTP, timestamps drift and events are sequenced incorrectly, corrupting the timeline.

distractors.A: NAT rules translate addresses; they do not alter log timestamps.
distractors.B: Dashboard styling has no effect on event ordering.
distractors.D: A query issue would not selectively reorder events that were captured correctly; skewed clocks would.

explanation.exam_pattern: Events out of order across devices = time-synchronization (NTP) problem.

references: CS0-003 1.1 - Log correlation and time synchronization

questions.stem: Traffic to an external host uses TCP 443, but the payload does not follow TLS and resembles an interactive shell. Which technique best identifies the true protocol?

options.text: Trusting the port number to name the service
Counting the number of packets exchanged
Reverse DNS lookup on the destination

explanation.correct: Port numbers are only conventions; adversaries tunnel other protocols over 443 to blend in. Deep packet inspection examines the actual payload structure to reveal the real application-layer protocol.

distractors.B: Mapping 443 to 'HTTPS' is exactly the assumption the attacker exploits; the port does not prove the protocol.
distractors.C: Packet counts reveal volume, not protocol identity.
distractors.D: Reverse DNS names the host, not the protocol riding the connection.

explanation.exam_pattern: Payload does not match the port's expected protocol = inspect at the application layer (DPI); do not trust the port.

references: CS0-003 1.2 - Protocol analysis (port vs. payload)

questions.stem: To detect unauthorized persistence on a server, an analyst wants to know what changed since deployment. Which comparison most directly surfaces unexpected startup items?

options.text: Reboot the server and time how long boot takes
Confirm the operating-system license is activated
Diff current autoruns/services against the known-good gold-image baseline
Read the server's physical asset tag

explanation.correct: Comparing current auto-start entries, services, and scheduled tasks against a trusted gold-image baseline reveals additions an attacker made for persistence that would otherwise blend in.

distractors.A: Boot time is a crude metric and will not identify which startup entries were added.
distractors.B: License activation is unrelated to persistence artifacts.
distractors.D: An asset tag identifies hardware, not software changes.

explanation.exam_pattern: Find unauthorized persistence = diff current configuration against a known-good baseline.

references: CS0-003 1.1 - Configuration baselines and integrity

questions.stem: An analyst is cataloging data sources and must label the host-based (endpoint) ones. Which TWO are endpoint telemetry sources rather than network telemetry? (Choose two.)

options.text: NetFlow records from a core router

explanation.correct: Sysmon and the Windows Security event log are generated on the endpoint and describe host activity (process creation, logons), making them host/endpoint telemetry.

distractors.B: NetFlow is collected from network devices and describes conversations between hosts, not on-host activity.
distractors.D: Firewall logs are network telemetry recording perimeter traffic decisions, not endpoint events.

explanation.exam_pattern: Host telemetry = generated ON the endpoint (Sysmon, Security log); network telemetry = flows, firewall, taps.

references: CS0-003 1.1 - Host vs. network telemetry sources

questions.stem: A SOC wants its detections to be the hardest for an adversary to evade. Per the Pyramid of Pain, detecting which indicator type is costliest for the adversary to change?

explanation.correct: In the Pyramid of Pain, TTPs sit at the apex; changing core behaviors forces the adversary to retool and relearn, far harder than swapping a hash, IP, or domain.

distractors.B: Hashes sit at the bottom - trivial to change by altering a single byte.
distractors.C: Domains are cheap to register and rotate, causing only minor disruption.
distractors.D: Adversaries rotate IP addresses easily, so blocking them causes little pain.

explanation.exam_pattern: Pyramid of Pain apex = TTPs; detecting behavior hurts adversaries most.

references: CS0-003 1.4 - Pyramid of Pain

questions.stem: A detection fires on the behavioral sequence of credential dumping followed by lateral movement, before any known-bad file is seen. Is this primarily an IOC or an IOA, and why?

options.text: An IOA, because it simply lists a blocked IP address
An IOC, because it is a signature of previously seen malware
An IOA, because it detects adversary behavior/intent in progress
An IOC, because a known file hash matched

explanation.correct: Indicators of attack describe adversary actions and intent (here, dumping credentials then moving laterally) and can catch novel tooling, unlike static indicators of compromise.

distractors.A: A blocked IP is a static IOC, not what fired here, and the scenario describes behavior.
distractors.B: A malware signature is an IOC; this detection is behavior-based and tool-agnostic.
distractors.D: No hash match is involved; the detection is behavioral, not a file artifact.

explanation.exam_pattern: Behavior/intent in progress = IOA; static artifact (hash/IP/domain) = IOC.

references: CS0-003 1.4 - Indicators of compromise vs. indicators of attack

questions.stem: A hospital wants to exchange vetted threat information with peer organizations in its own industry sector. Which type of body is purpose-built for this sharing?

options.text: An ISAC (Information Sharing and Analysis Center)

explanation.correct: ISACs are sector-specific communities (for example H-ISAC for health, FS-ISAC for finance) that enable trusted sharing of threat intelligence among members of the same industry.

distractors.A: A certificate authority issues digital certificates, unrelated to intel sharing.
distractors.B: A CDN distributes web content; it is not a threat-sharing community.
distractors.D: A print service has no role in threat-intelligence exchange.

explanation.exam_pattern: Sector-based trusted threat sharing = ISAC.

references: CS0-003 1.4 - Intelligence sharing (ISAC)

questions.stem: An analyst maps observed activity to MITRE ATT&CK and files it under the Exfiltration tactic. In ATT&CK terms, what does the corresponding technique describe?

options.text: The monetary cost of the breach
The legal attribution of the actor
The specific method used to achieve the tactic's goal

explanation.correct: In ATT&CK a tactic is the adversary's goal (the 'why', e.g., Exfiltration) and a technique is the 'how' - the specific method used to accomplish that goal, such as exfiltration over a C2 channel.

distractors.A: Breach cost is a business-impact metric, not an ATT&CK technique.
distractors.B: ATT&CK catalogs behavior, not legal attribution.
distractors.C: The overall goal is the tactic, not the technique.

explanation.exam_pattern: ATT&CK: tactic = why/goal; technique = how/method.

references: CS0-003 1.4 - MITRE ATT&CK (tactics vs. techniques)

questions.stem: A CISO requests long-horizon analysis of adversary trends and motivations to guide multi-year security investment. Which category of threat intelligence best serves this?

explanation.correct: Strategic intelligence is high-level, largely non-technical analysis of trends, motivations, and risk that informs executive decisions and long-term investment.

distractors.A: Raw packet captures are operational data far below the strategic altitude a CISO needs.
distractors.C: Tactical intelligence focuses on adversary TTPs for defenders and SOC operations, not executive strategy.
distractors.D: Technical indicators are atomic, short-lived artifacts for detection, not strategic planning.

explanation.exam_pattern: Executive trends / long-term investment = strategic intel; SOC TTPs = tactical.

references: CS0-003 1.4 - Threat-intelligence levels (strategic/tactical/technical)

questions.stem: A single, unverified post on an open forum claims a named nation-state hit your industry. How should an analyst weight this before alerting leadership to the attribution?

options.text: Assign low confidence and corroborate before attributing
Discard all single-source reporting as useless
Immediately attribute the activity to that nation-state
Raise the organization's threat level to maximum at once

explanation.correct: A lone uncorroborated open-source claim warrants low confidence; responsible analysis seeks corroboration and avoids premature attribution, which can misdirect response and damage credibility.

distractors.B: Single-source tips still have value as leads; they are triaged by confidence, not discarded outright.
distractors.C: Attributing from one unverified source is premature and risks acting on false information.
distractors.D: Maxing the threat level on one unverified post is a disproportionate overreaction.

explanation.exam_pattern: Uncorroborated single source = low confidence; corroborate before attributing.

references: CS0-003 1.4 - Confidence levels and attribution

questions.stem: An intrusion shows months of stealthy dwell time, custom malware, and patient espionage against intellectual property. Which threat-actor profile does this best match?

explanation.correct: Long dwell time, custom tooling, heavy resourcing, and espionage goals are hallmarks of an advanced persistent threat, typically nation-state sponsored.

distractors.A: Hacktivists seek visibility and disruption, not stealthy long-term espionage.
distractors.B: Script kiddies use off-the-shelf tools opportunistically and lack the patience and custom capability shown.
distractors.D: An accidental insider causes unintentional harm, not a sustained custom-malware campaign.

explanation.exam_pattern: Stealth + persistence + custom tools + espionage = nation-state/APT.

references: CS0-003 1.4 - Threat actors and motivations

questions.stem: A SOC wants to automate ingestion of a partner's machine-readable threat intelligence. Which TWO standards are designed specifically for expressing and exchanging CTI? (Choose two.)

explanation.correct: STIX is the standardized language for representing threat intelligence, and TAXII is the transport protocol for sharing STIX content between systems - together they enable automated CTI exchange.

distractors.B: SMTP transports email, not structured threat intelligence.
distractors.C: SNMP manages and monitors network devices; it is not a CTI standard.

explanation.exam_pattern: Structured CTI exchange = STIX (language) + TAXII (transport).

references: CS0-003 1.4 - Intelligence standards (STIX/TAXII)

questions.stem: An open threat feed keeps flagging IP addresses that were sinkholed months ago, generating false positives. Which intelligence quality issue does this illustrate?

explanation.correct: Indicators have a limited useful life; feeds that fail to age out stale IOCs lose timeliness and relevance, producing false positives on infrastructure that is no longer malicious.

distractors.A: The feed is delivering data fine; the problem is indicator freshness, not transport.
distractors.C: Bandwidth does not affect whether an indicator is still current.
distractors.D: Encryption strength has nothing to do with stale-indicator false positives.

explanation.exam_pattern: Stale indicators causing false positives = timeliness/relevance (aging) problem.

references: CS0-003 1.4 - Intelligence quality (timeliness/relevance)

questions.stem: A team proactively searches for undetected adversaries by forming and testing a specific assumption about attacker behavior, rather than waiting for alerts. What is this called?

explanation.correct: Threat hunting is proactive and hypothesis-driven: the hunter states a testable assumption (e.g., 'an adversary is using WMI for lateral movement') and investigates telemetry to prove or disprove it.

distractors.A: Signature-based alerting is reactive, firing only on known patterns - the opposite of proactive hunting.
distractors.B: Vulnerability scanning finds weaknesses, not active adversary behavior.
distractors.D: Patch management remediates vulnerabilities; it does not hunt for intruders.

explanation.exam_pattern: Proactive + testable assumption about attacker behavior = hypothesis-driven hunting.

references: CS0-003 1.4 - Threat hunting (hypothesis-driven)

questions.stem: When scoping a hunt, a team prioritizes adversary behaviors over lists of file hashes and IP addresses. Why is focusing on TTPs more durable?

options.text: Behaviors are costlier for adversaries to change than atomic indicators
IP addresses uniquely identify an adversary forever
Hashes never change between malware builds
Behaviors are easier to paste into a blocklist

explanation.correct: TTPs reflect how adversaries operate and are expensive to alter, so detections built on behavior remain effective even when the attacker swaps hashes, IPs, or domains.

distractors.B: Adversaries rotate IPs constantly; an IP does not permanently identify anyone.
distractors.C: Hashes change with every recompile or minor edit, making them fragile.
distractors.D: Ease of blocklisting describes atomic IOCs, not the durability of behavioral detection.

explanation.exam_pattern: Hunt behaviors (TTPs) for lasting detections; IOCs are ephemeral.

references: CS0-003 1.4 - Threat hunting focus (TTPs over IOCs)

questions.stem: A hunt lead wants to visualize which MITRE ATT&CK techniques the team can currently detect and where the blind spots are. Which approach fits best?

options.text: Build an ATT&CK Navigator coverage heatmap of existing detections
Measure average CPU load on the SIEM
Count the total alerts fired last month
Tally the number of firewall rules

explanation.correct: Mapping current detections onto an ATT&CK Navigator layer produces a coverage heatmap that highlights which techniques are covered and which gaps warrant new hunts and analytics.

distractors.B: SIEM CPU load is an operational metric, not detection coverage.
distractors.C: Raw alert counts say nothing about which techniques are or are not covered.
distractors.D: Firewall rule counts do not map to adversary techniques or detection gaps.

explanation.exam_pattern: Detection coverage/gaps across techniques = map to ATT&CK (Navigator heatmap).

references: CS0-003 1.4 - ATT&CK-driven hunting and coverage

questions.stem: A completed hunt finds no active compromise but reveals that a key lateral-movement technique was invisible to current tooling. What is the primary value delivered?

options.text: The environment is now permanently secure
The hunt failed and should not be repeated
No action is warranted since nothing was found
A new detection/analytic closes a visibility gap

explanation.correct: A hunt that finds nothing still delivers value by exposing visibility gaps; converting the hunt logic into a durable detection improves future coverage even without an active incident.

distractors.A: No single hunt makes an environment permanently secure; threats evolve.
distractors.B: Discovering a blind spot is a successful outcome, not a failure.
distractors.C: Finding a visibility gap demands action - building the missing detection.

explanation.exam_pattern: No compromise found but a gap exposed = turn the hunt into a new detection.

references: CS0-003 1.4 - Threat hunting (improving detections)

questions.stem: While hunting, a team discovers forgotten internet-facing servers running unused services. Beyond detection, which hunt outcome does hardening or removing these represent?

explanation.correct: Identifying and decommissioning or hardening exposed, unnecessary services shrinks the attack surface - an intended secondary benefit of proactive hunting.

distractors.A: Attack-surface reduction is unrelated to shortening log retention.
distractors.B: Removing exposure reduces, not increases, the opportunity for dwell time.
distractors.D: Closing exposures shrinks the blast radius rather than expanding it.

explanation.exam_pattern: Hunt finds and removes needless exposure = attack-surface reduction.

references: CS0-003 1.4 - Threat hunting (attack-surface reduction)

questions.stem: A hunt program is founded on the premise that adversaries may already be inside and evading existing controls. Which mindset does this reflect?

explanation.correct: Threat hunting adopts an assume-breach posture: rather than trusting that controls kept everyone out, hunters actively look for adversaries presumed to already be present.

distractors.A: Implicit trust is the opposite stance and undermines hunting.
distractors.C: Security through obscurity hides details; it is not a hunting premise.
distractors.D: Default-allow is a permissive access posture, not a hunting mindset.

explanation.exam_pattern: Hunting presumes intruders are already present = assume-breach.

references: CS0-003 1.4 - Threat hunting (assume-breach)

questions.stem: To find anomalies across thousands of endpoints, a hunter aggregates one data field and investigates its rarest values. Which analytic technique is being used?

explanation.correct: Stacking counts how often each value occurs across hosts so the hunter can examine the long-tail outliers - rare parent-child pairs or unusual binaries - that often reveal malicious activity.

distractors.A: Load balancing distributes traffic; it is not a hunting technique.
distractors.B: Full-disk encryption protects data at rest and is unrelated to analytics.
distractors.D: Signature matching detects known patterns, not statistically rare outliers.

explanation.exam_pattern: Aggregate and investigate the rarest values = frequency analysis / stacking (LFO).

references: CS0-003 1.4 - Hunting techniques (stacking/frequency)

questions.stem: A new report details an APT's specific persistence and lateral-movement techniques against your sector. How should a hunt team best use it?

options.text: Ignore it unless an alert fires
Form a hypothesis that those TTPs are present and hunt for them
Immediately rebuild every server from scratch
Block the entire internet at the firewall

explanation.correct: Fresh, relevant intelligence is an ideal seed for an intel-driven hunt: the team hypothesizes the described TTPs may be present and searches telemetry for that specific behavior.

distractors.A: Waiting for an alert abandons the proactive value of the intelligence.
distractors.C: Rebuilding all servers is disproportionate and does not confirm whether the TTPs are present.
distractors.D: Blocking all internet access is operationally untenable and does not test the hypothesis.

explanation.exam_pattern: Relevant CTI on actor TTPs = seed an intel-driven hunt hypothesis.

references: CS0-003 1.4 - Intel-driven threat hunting

questions.stem: A hunt team is deciding what should inform a high-value, testable hypothesis. Which TWO inputs are the strongest sources? (Choose two.)

options.text: Recent threat intel on an actor's TTPs targeting your sector
An unexplained deviation from your environment's baseline
The calendar date of the next compliance audit

explanation.correct: Strong hypotheses are grounded in relevant adversary intelligence and in observed anomalies against a known baseline - both point to concrete, testable behaviors to investigate.

distractors.C: An audit date is a compliance milestone, not a basis for a behavioral hypothesis.
distractors.D: Marketing material is promotional, not evidence of adversary behavior to hunt.

explanation.exam_pattern: Good hunt hypotheses come from relevant CTI and baseline anomalies.

references: CS0-003 1.4 - Forming hunt hypotheses

questions.stem: A host connects to the same external IP every 60 seconds, each time sending a small, uniform payload, around the clock. Which malicious behavior does this most indicate?

options.text: A printer keep-alive on the LAN

explanation.correct: Regular, periodic callbacks of uniform size to a single external host are classic C2 beaconing, where an implant checks in with its controller on a fixed interval.

distractors.B: Printer keep-alives stay on the LAN, not to an external IP around the clock.
distractors.C: OS updates are intermittent and bursty, not a precise per-minute heartbeat to one IP.
distractors.D: DNS resolution targets resolvers with varied queries, not a fixed 60-second uniform callback.

explanation.exam_pattern: Fixed-interval, uniform callbacks to one external host = C2 beaconing.

references: CS0-003 1.2 - Network indicators (C2/beaconing)

questions.stem: A single internal IP rapidly opens connections to hundreds of different ports across many hosts within seconds. Which activity does this most likely represent?

explanation.correct: One source touching many ports and hosts in a short burst is the signature of a scan - reconnaissance to enumerate reachable services, often preceding an attack.

distractors.A: A license check contacts a specific vendor endpoint, not a broad port sweep.
distractors.C: Backups target specific storage endpoints, not a sweep across many ports and hosts.
distractors.D: Time sync contacts a few NTP servers on UDP 123, not hundreds of ports.

explanation.exam_pattern: One source -> many ports/hosts fast = scanning/recon.

references: CS0-003 1.2 - Network indicators (scanning)

questions.stem: An analyst sees a host issuing a high volume of DNS queries for long, random-looking subdomains of a single registered domain. Which technique is most consistent with this?

options.text: DNS tunneling for exfiltration or C2

explanation.correct: Encoding data into long, high-entropy subdomain labels and sending many queries to one authoritative domain is characteristic of DNS tunneling, used to exfiltrate data or carry C2 past egress filters.

distractors.A: NTP amplification abuses UDP 123 reflection, not crafted DNS subdomains.
distractors.C: CDN caching resolves normal hostnames; it does not produce floods of random high-entropy subdomains.
distractors.D: ARP spoofing manipulates layer-2 address mappings on the LAN, unrelated to DNS query content.

explanation.exam_pattern: Many long/random subdomains of one domain = DNS tunneling (exfil/C2).

references: CS0-003 1.2 - Network indicators (DNS tunneling/exfiltration)

questions.stem: After eradicating malware, an analyst wants to ensure it will not relaunch at logon. Which host artifact is a common persistence mechanism to inspect first?

options.text: A Run/RunOnce registry key or a new scheduled task

explanation.correct: Autostart locations such as the Run/RunOnce registry keys and scheduled tasks are frequent persistence mechanisms that relaunch malware at logon or on a trigger and must be checked during eradication.

distractors.A: Display resolution has no bearing on program persistence.
distractors.B: Recycle-bin size does not relaunch software.
distractors.C: Wallpaper settings do not execute code at startup.

explanation.exam_pattern: Relaunch-at-logon persistence = Run keys, scheduled tasks, services, startup folder.

references: CS0-003 1.2 - Host indicators (persistence)

questions.stem: A spoofed message passed SPF checks yet DMARC still failed. Which explanation best accounts for this outcome?

options.text: SPF authenticated the envelope domain, which did not align with the From-header domain
SPF and DMARC are the same check, so the result is contradictory
DMARC failed only because the message had no attachments
DMARC requires the message to be encrypted in transit with TLS

explanation.correct: DMARC requires SPF or DKIM to pass AND to align with the visible From domain. A message can pass SPF on its envelope (Return-Path) domain yet fail DMARC when that domain does not align with the spoofed From header.

distractors.B: SPF validates the sending IP/envelope while DMARC adds alignment and policy - distinct checks, so the result is not contradictory.
distractors.C: Attachments have no bearing on DMARC evaluation.
distractors.D: DMARC concerns authentication and identifier alignment, not transport encryption such as STARTTLS.

explanation.exam_pattern: SPF pass but DMARC fail = identifier-alignment failure with the From domain.

references: CS0-003 1.2 - Email indicators (SPF/DKIM/DMARC)

questions.stem: Triaging a suspected phish, an analyst compares the message headers. Which finding most strongly supports a spoofing attempt?

options.text: The email arrived during business hours
The From domain differs from the Return-Path, and Reply-To points to an unrelated address
The subject line is written in all capitals
The message contains an image attachment

explanation.correct: A mismatch between the displayed From domain and the Return-Path, combined with a Reply-To that redirects responses to an unrelated attacker-controlled address, is a hallmark of spoofing.

distractors.A: Delivery timing does not indicate forgery.
distractors.C: A capitalized subject may signal spam tone but does not evidence header spoofing.
distractors.D: Image attachments are common in legitimate mail and are not themselves proof of spoofing.

explanation.exam_pattern: From vs. Return-Path mismatch plus a suspicious Reply-To = spoofing indicators.

references: CS0-003 1.2 - Email header analysis

questions.stem: An analyst finds a process launched as 'powershell.exe -nop -w hidden -enc <long Base64 string>'. Which adversary technique does the -enc argument indicate?

options.text: Command obfuscation / defense evasion via a Base64-encoded command

explanation.correct: The -EncodedCommand (-enc) switch runs a Base64-encoded command, which attackers use to obscure intent and evade simple string-based detection - an obfuscation/defense-evasion technique.

distractors.A: Certificate pinning validates TLS endpoints and is unrelated to PowerShell arguments.
distractors.B: Password hashing protects credentials at rest, not command content passed to PowerShell.
distractors.D: This encodes a command string, not the disk; no volume encryption is involved.

explanation.exam_pattern: powershell -enc <Base64> = obfuscated command (defense evasion).

references: CS0-003 1.2 - Obfuscation and defense evasion

questions.stem: An EDR shows a process named svchost.exe running from C:\Users\Public\ and not spawned by services.exe. Which malicious technique best explains this?

options.text: Masquerading as a legitimate system process

explanation.correct: Genuine svchost.exe runs from System32 and is started by services.exe; a same-named binary executing from a user-writable path with the wrong parent is masquerading to blend in with trusted processes.

distractors.A: Certificate renewal does not spawn a mislocated svchost.exe.
distractors.B: Profile sync does not run system-process names from user-writable directories.
distractors.C: A normal service start originates from System32 under services.exe, not a public user folder.

explanation.exam_pattern: Legit process name in the wrong path / with the wrong parent = masquerading.

references: CS0-003 1.2 - Host indicators (masquerading)

questions.stem: An analyst reviews a host where built-in Windows tools were abused to download and run a payload while evading detection. Which TWO are commonly abused living-off-the-land binaries? (Choose two.)

explanation.correct: certutil.exe can download and decode files, and mshta.exe can execute remote HTA/script content; both are legitimate signed binaries attackers abuse to operate without dropping obvious malware.

distractors.B: notepad.exe is a text editor with no download or script-execution capability to abuse this way.
distractors.D: winver.exe merely displays the Windows version and cannot fetch or run payloads.

explanation.exam_pattern: Signed built-ins abused to download/execute (certutil, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32) = LOLBins.

references: CS0-003 1.2 - Living-off-the-land / abused utilities

questions.stem: A team needs one platform to aggregate logs from firewalls, servers, and endpoints and correlate them to detect multi-stage attacks. Which tool category fits?

explanation.correct: A SIEM centralizes and normalizes logs from many sources and applies correlation rules to surface multi-stage activity that individual devices would miss in isolation.

distractors.A: A label printer produces physical labels and has no log-analysis function.
distractors.C: A load balancer distributes traffic and does not perform cross-source correlation.
distractors.D: A password vault stores secrets; it does not correlate security events.

explanation.exam_pattern: Aggregate + correlate logs from many sources = SIEM.

references: CS0-003 1.3 - SIEM (correlation)

questions.stem: After a SIEM detects phishing, leadership wants containment steps - enrich the IOC, open a ticket, and isolate the host - to run automatically via a playbook. Which capability provides this?

explanation.correct: SOAR adds orchestration and automation: playbooks execute response actions (enrichment, ticketing, host isolation) automatically, extending the SIEM's detection with action.

distractors.A: A dashboard visualizes data; it does not execute automated response playbooks.
distractors.B: A syslog collector forwards logs; it does not orchestrate response.
distractors.D: A packet broker distributes traffic to tools and performs no response automation.

explanation.exam_pattern: Automated response playbooks after detection = SOAR (SIEM detects, SOAR acts).

references: CS0-003 1.5 - SOAR / orchestration

questions.stem: An analyst must remotely isolate a compromised laptop and kill a malicious process based on its behavior, not just a signature. Which tool provides this on the endpoint?

explanation.correct: EDR continuously monitors endpoint behavior, detects suspicious activity, and supports response actions such as isolating the host and terminating processes remotely.

distractors.A: A DHCP server assigns IP addresses; it has no endpoint-response role.
distractors.B: A spam filter screens email and cannot isolate a host or kill a process.
distractors.D: A network tap copies traffic for inspection but cannot act on an endpoint.

explanation.exam_pattern: Behavioral endpoint detection + remote isolate/kill = EDR.

references: CS0-003 1.3 - Endpoint security (EDR)

questions.stem: An analyst has a packet capture and needs to reassemble a TCP conversation to confirm credentials were sent in cleartext. Which tool and feature fit best?

options.text: tcpdump with no filter printing to the console
Starting a fresh Wireshark capture on a new interface

explanation.correct: Wireshark's Follow TCP Stream reassembles a flow's payload into a readable transcript, letting the analyst confirm whether credentials traversed the network unencrypted.

distractors.B: A SIEM rule correlates log events, not packet payloads inside a capture file.
distractors.C: tcpdump streaming raw packets to the console is poorly suited to reassembling and reading an application-layer transcript.
distractors.D: Starting a new capture does not analyze the existing pcap that already contains the conversation.

explanation.exam_pattern: Reassemble/read a conversation's payload from a pcap = Wireshark Follow TCP Stream.

references: CS0-003 1.3 - Packet analysis (Wireshark)

questions.stem: On a headless Linux server, an analyst must capture only traffic to host 10.0.0.5 on port 443 and save it for later analysis. Which approach is appropriate?

options.text: Open Wireshark's GUI on the server console
Run a full port scan of 10.0.0.5
Disable the server's NIC to force a capture
Run tcpdump with a filter 'host 10.0.0.5 and port 443', writing to a pcap file

explanation.correct: tcpdump is the right CLI tool for a headless host; a Berkeley Packet Filter ('host 10.0.0.5 and port 443') limits capture to the traffic of interest, and -w writes it to a pcap for later analysis.

distractors.A: A headless server has no GUI, so launching Wireshark's interface there is not viable.
distractors.B: A port scan generates traffic and enumerates services; it does not capture the existing conversation.
distractors.C: Disabling the NIC stops traffic entirely, preventing any capture.

explanation.exam_pattern: Headless, filtered capture to a file = tcpdump with a BPF filter and -w.

references: CS0-003 1.3 - Packet capture (tcpdump/BPF)

questions.stem: A SOC automates tier-1 phishing triage with a playbook. Which benefit most directly results from replacing the manual, repetitive steps?

options.text: No further need for any analysts
Guaranteed elimination of all false positives
Automatic repeal of all security policies
Faster, more consistent response with fewer human errors

explanation.correct: Automation executes repetitive steps quickly and identically every time, lowering mean time to respond and reducing the human errors that creep into manual, high-volume work.

distractors.A: Automation augments analysts for higher-value work; it does not remove the need for human judgment.
distractors.B: Automation speeds and standardizes triage but does not eliminate false positives, which stem from detection logic.
distractors.C: Automation enforces process; it does not repeal security policy.

explanation.exam_pattern: Automation benefits = speed, consistency, fewer errors (lower MTTR).

references: CS0-003 1.5 - Benefits of automation/orchestration

questions.stem: An analyst must check 500 file hashes against a threat-intel API and summarize the hits. Which approach is most efficient and repeatable?

options.text: Reboot the SIEM to refresh its cache
Email the list to the vendor and wait for a reply
Write a script that queries the API and parses the results programmatically
Paste each hash into a web form by hand

explanation.correct: Scripting (for example Python calling the API) automates the bulk lookups and result parsing, delivering a fast, consistent, repeatable process that manual effort cannot match at that volume.

distractors.A: Rebooting the SIEM does nothing to enrich external hash reputation.
distractors.B: Emailing the vendor introduces delay and provides no structured, immediate result.
distractors.D: Manually submitting 500 hashes is slow, error-prone, and not repeatable.

explanation.exam_pattern: Repetitive bulk enrichment at scale = script against the API.

references: CS0-003 1.3 - Scripting/automation for analysis

questions.stem: A correlation rule floods analysts with alerts from a known-good vulnerability scanner, causing alert fatigue. Which tuning action best reduces noise without hiding real threats?

options.text: Allow-list the scanner's source and refine the rule's logic/thresholds
Raise every rule's severity to critical
Disable all logging on the affected sensors

explanation.correct: Tuning - allow-listing the authorized scanner and tightening rule conditions or thresholds - removes predictable benign noise while preserving detection of genuine anomalies.

distractors.A: Removing the correlation engine eliminates detection entirely, not just the noise.
distractors.C: Escalating every rule to critical worsens fatigue and buries true positives.
distractors.D: Disabling logging creates blind spots and destroys the evidence trail.

explanation.exam_pattern: Benign source flooding alerts = tune/allow-list that source; do not kill logging.

references: CS0-003 1.5 - Tuning / reducing false positives

questions.stem: An analyst received a suspicious attachment and must examine it without endangering the environment. Which TWO actions are appropriate? (Choose two.)

options.text: Detonate it in an isolated sandbox
Compute its hash and check reputation/threat intel
Forward it to all staff as a warning with the file attached
Open it on the analyst's own workstation to see what it does

explanation.correct: Detonating the file in an isolated sandbox reveals its behavior safely, and hashing it for a reputation/threat-intel lookup identifies known-malicious files - both contain risk while yielding intelligence.

distractors.C: Forwarding the live attachment to all staff spreads the threat and invites accidental execution.
distractors.D: Opening it on a production workstation risks executing the very malware under investigation.

explanation.exam_pattern: Analyze suspect files safely = sandbox detonation + hash/reputation lookup; never open live.

references: CS0-003 1.3 - Email/malware analysis (sandboxing)

questions.stem: An analyst must identify precisely which OS patches are missing on a fleet of hardened Linux servers. Which scan approach yields the most accurate patch-level results?

options.text: An external unauthenticated scan from the internet

explanation.correct: Credentialed scans log in to the host and read installed package versions, registry/config, and patch state directly, giving accurate missing-patch detection with few false positives.

distractors.B: Passive monitoring observes traffic and never queries host patch levels, so it cannot enumerate missing patches.
distractors.C: Non-credentialed scans only infer from exposed services and banners, so patch state is estimated and false positives are common.
distractors.D: An external unauthenticated scan sees only internet-facing services, not the host's internal patch inventory.

explanation.exam_pattern: Accurate patch/config detail with low false positives points to credentialed scanning.

references: CS0-003 2.1 Scanning methods: credentialed vs non-credentialed

questions.stem: A company's sales laptops are frequently off-network and rarely online long enough for scheduled network scans. Which scanning method best ensures these endpoints are assessed?

options.text: A passive sensor on the core switch

explanation.correct: A locally installed agent collects data while the device is offline and reports results when the laptop reconnects, so intermittent and roaming assets are still assessed.

distractors.B: A passive core-switch sensor only sees devices while they generate traffic through that switch, missing offline laptops.
distractors.C: External perimeter scanning cannot reach endpoints that are off the corporate network or behind other NAT.
distractors.D: Agentless network scanning requires the host to be online and reachable during the scan window, which roaming laptops often are not.

explanation.exam_pattern: Intermittent/roaming or BYOD endpoints favor agent-based over agentless scanning.

references: CS0-003 2.1 Scanning methods: agent vs agentless

questions.stem: A plant's legacy SCADA controllers have crashed when probed by active scanners, yet management still wants vulnerability visibility. Which approach minimizes operational disruption?

options.text: Passive network monitoring of the OT segment
Brute-force service enumeration of each controller
An aggressive active scan during production hours
Installing a scanning agent on each PLC

explanation.correct: Passive monitoring inspects mirrored traffic without sending probes to fragile OT/ICS devices, so it gathers vulnerability intelligence without risking a crash.

distractors.B: Brute-force enumeration sends even more probing traffic, increasing the chance of disrupting the controllers.
distractors.C: Aggressive active scanning is exactly what crashes these fragile controllers, and running it during production magnifies the impact.
distractors.D: Legacy PLCs typically cannot host modern scanning agents, and installing software on them risks instability.

explanation.exam_pattern: Fragile/OT/ICS systems that crash under probing call for passive scanning.

references: CS0-003 2.1 Special considerations: fragile systems and operational technology

questions.stem: After a new web app launches in the DMZ, the team wants to see exactly what an unauthenticated internet attacker could enumerate. Which scan vantage point fits?

options.text: A host agent scan on the web server
An external scan launched from outside the perimeter
An internal credentialed scan from the server VLAN
A passive sensor on an internal trunk port

explanation.correct: An external scan originates outside the firewall and shows only what is reachable from the internet, mirroring an outside attacker's view of the DMZ asset.

distractors.A: A host agent reports the full internal state of the server, not the limited external attack surface.
distractors.C: An internal credentialed scan sees far more than an external attacker could and bypasses perimeter filtering, so it does not represent the attacker's view.
distractors.D: An internal passive sensor observes internal traffic and cannot represent an unauthenticated internet attacker's perspective.

explanation.exam_pattern: Attacker's internet-facing perspective means an external scan from outside the perimeter.

references: CS0-003 2.1 Scanning methods: internal vs external

questions.stem: A non-credentialed scan of a database server returned many 'potential' findings that the DBA says were patched months ago. What best explains these results?

options.text: The host silently dropped all scan traffic
Credentialed scans inherently miss applied patches
The scanner had no vulnerability plugin/feed installed
False positives caused by the scanner lacking authenticated host visibility

explanation.correct: Without credentials the scanner infers vulnerabilities from version banners and exposed behavior; back-ported or vendor patches that do not change the banner are flagged as 'potential', producing false positives.

distractors.A: If all traffic were dropped the scanner would report the host as down or unresponsive, not list service-level findings.
